Given a list of object IDs, calls :meth:`~dxpy.api.system_describe_data_objects`.

    Example::

        describe(["file-1234", "workflow-5678"])

    Note: If id_or_link is a list and **kwargs contains a "fields" parameter, these
    fields will be returned in the response for each data object in addition to the
    fields included by default. Additionally, describe options can be provided for
    each data object class in the "classDescribeOptions" kwargs argument. See
    https://documentation.dnanexus.com/developer/api/system-methods#api-method-system-describedataobjects
    for input parameters used with the multiple object describe method.
    '''
    # If this is a list, extract the ids.
    # TODO: modify the procedure to use project ID when possible
    if isinstance(id_or_link, basestring) or is_dxlink(id_or_link):
        handler = get_handler(id_or_link)
        return handler.describe(**kwargs)
    else:
        links = []
        for link in id_or_link:
            # If this entry is a dxlink, then get the id.
            if is_dxlink(link):
                # Guaranteed by is_dxlink that one of the following will work
                if isinstance(link['$dnanexus_link'], basestring):
                    link = link['$dnanexus_link']
                else:
                    link = link['$dnanexus_link']['id']
            links.append(link)
---GETSTATE_BODY
        Note that this function is shorthand for:

            dxclass.describe()["state"]

        '''

        return self.describe(fields={'state'}, **kwargs)["state"]

    def describe(self, incl_properties=False, incl_details=False, fields=None, default_fields=None, **kwargs):
        """
        :param fields: set of fields to include in the output, for
            example ``{'name', 'modified'}``. The field ``id`` is always
            implicitly included. If ``fields`` is specified, the default
            fields are not included (that is, only the fields specified
            here, and ``id``, are included) unless ``default_fields`` is
            additionally set to True.
        :type fields: set or sequence of str
        :param default_fields: if True, include the default fields in
            addition to fields requested in ``fields``, if any; if
            False, only the fields specified in ``fields``, if any, are
            returned (defaults to False if ``fields`` is specified, True
            otherwise)
        :type default_fields: bool
        :param incl_properties: if true, includes the properties of the
            object in the output (deprecated; use

UNIT dxglobalworkflow.py::DXGlobalWorkflow.get_underlying_workflow (lines 197-227)
 - C8.S1, lines 215-216: the per-region cache check never hits, because `self._workflows_by_region` is only initialised in `__init__` and never written. Every call rebuilds the underlying handler and, when `describe_output` is not passed, makes a fresh global-workflow describe (lines 218-219).
 - C8.S1, line 226: the cache write goes to the wrong attribute (`_workflow_desc_by_region`) and stores a DXWorkflow handler, and line 227 builds a second DXWorkflow for the same ID instead of returning the one just built. The intended cache is therefore never populated.
 - Caller evidence: src/python/dxpy/cli/exec_io.py:777 calls `_get_input_name` once per `--input`. For stage-qualified keys (containing '.'), the new handler's `stages` access goes through `DXDataObject.__getattr__` (bindings/__init__.py:94-105), which triggers a describe API call each time.

UNIT dxglobalworkflow.py::DXGlobalWorkflow.describe_underlying_workflow (lines 163-195)
 - C8.S1, lines 181-182 and 194: the description cache is never hit. Line 194 overwrites the dict `_workflow_desc_by_region` with a single workflow description rather than storing it under `region`, so `region in self._workflow_desc_by_region` checks the description's keys and misses. Each call therefore pays the describe at line 185 (if `describe_output` is absent) and the underlying `dxworkflow.describe()` at line 193.

UNIT dxglobalworkflow.py::DXGlobalWorkflow._get_run_input (lines 256-265)
 - C8.S1, line 264: `get_underlying_workflow(region)` is called without `describe_output`, and because of the cache bug above it re-describes the global workflow and the underlying workflow on every run. The region is also re-fetched via `project_describe` (lines 262-263) on every call. Both repeat work whose answers do not change for a given handler.

UNIT dxanalysis.py::DXAnalysis.wait_on_done (lines 111-140)
 - C9.S1 (low confidence), lines 124 and 139: the loop polls the API with a full describe round trip every fixed 2 seconds (default `interval=2`) for up to a 7-day timeout. A longer or backing-off interval would reach the same decision with far fewer requests, so the extra calls are arguably unnecessary.

UNIT dxjob.py::DXJob.wait_on_done (lines 311-340)
 - C9.S1 (low confidence), lines 324 and 339: same fixed 2-second polling of `job_describe` as the analysis version, with the same argument that most polls return an unchanged state.

UNIT search.py::_find (lines 73-108)
 - C3.S5, lines 97-108: the loop only checks `num_results == limit` after a new element is pulled from the page. When a page is exhausted exactly at `limit` and `resp["next"]` is set, the generator still issues another API request (line 104-105) and fetches a page of up to `min(2*limit, 1000)` records, which is then discarded at line 98-99. The limit check should run before fetching the next page.
 - C9.S2, lines 106: page size doubles on every request regardless of how many results are still needed, so limited searches pull more records across the API boundary than the consumer ever reads.

UNIT search.py::_org_find (lines 759-782)
 - C9.S2 and C3.S5, lines 769-770 and 772-782: the `limit` in the query is used only as the initial page size, and the generator never stops at it. Any caller that passes `limit` and consumes the generator fully (e.g. `list(...)`) pages through every matching result. This is the same loop-without-early-exit pattern, with extra API fetches.

UNIT search.py::org_find_apps (lines 1002-1005)
 - C9.S2, lines 1002-1005: `limit` is written into the query and passed to `_org_find` (line 1005) without a cap on the number of yielded results, so the caller's limit does not bound the data fetched. See the `_org_find` entry above for the mechanism.

UNIT mount_all_inputs.py::_gen_helper_dict (lines 49-72)
 - C8.S4, lines 55-56: the input JSON file is re-read and re-parsed via `analyze_bash_vars`, which calls `get_job_input_filenames` again (utils/file_load_utils.py:366, file read at 211-215). The caller already holds the parsed `inputs` from the first read in `mount_all_inputs` (line 129), and this function uses it only for its keys.

UNIT download_all_inputs.py::_gen_helper_dict (lines 82-105)
 - C8.S4, lines 88-89: same redundant re-read and re-parse of job_input.json through `analyze_bash_vars` (utils/file_load_utils.py:366). The `inputs` parameter already contains the parsed data needed for the keys.

UNIT mount_all_inputs.py::mount_all_inputs (lines 116-164)
 - C10.S2, line 125: `subprocess.check_output(["mkdir", mount_dir])` spawns an external process where `os.mkdir` does the same work in-process.
 - C10.S2, lines 152-153: `subprocess.check_output(["id", "-u"])` and `["id", "-g"]` each spawn a process, where `os.getuid()` and `os.getgid()` return the same values without any process creation.
 - C1.S5, line 161: `subprocess.call(["find", mount_dir, "-name", "*"])` walks the entire dxfuse mount and only echoes the listing to the log. The `-name "*"` filter matches everything, so it adds nothing. Walking a FUSE mount can also trigger metadata fetches for every file.

        '''
        :param stage: A number for the stage index (for the nth stage, starting from 0), or a string of the stage index, name, or ID

        :param edit_version: if provided, the edit version of the workflow that should be modified; if not provided, the current edit version will be used (optional)

def wait_on_done(self, interval=2, timeout=3600*24*7, **kwargs):
        '''
        :param interval: Number of seconds between queries to the job's state
        :type interval: integer
        :param timeout: Maximum amount of time to wait, in seconds, until the job is done running
        :type timeout: integer
        :raises: :exc:`~dxpy.exceptions.DXError` if the timeout is reached before the job has finished running, or :exc:`dxpy.exceptions.DXJobFailureError` if the job fails

        Waits until the job has finished running.
        '''

        elapsed = 0
        while True:
            state = self._get_state(**kwargs)
            if state == "done":
                break
            if state == "failed":
                desc = self.describe(**kwargs)
                err_msg = "Job has failed because of {failureReason}: {failureMessage}".format(**desc)
                if desc.get("failureFrom") != None and desc["failureFrom"]["id"] != desc["id"]:
                    err_msg += " (failure from {id})".format(id=desc['failureFrom']['id'])
                raise DXJobFailureError(err_msg)
            if state == "terminated":
                raise DXJobFailureError("Job was terminated.")

            if elapsed >= timeout or elapsed < 0:
                raise DXJobFailureError("Reached timeout while waiting for the job to finish")

            time.sleep(interval)
            elapsed += interval

def get_first_pos_of_char(char, string):
    '''
    :param char: The character to find
    :type char: string
    :param string: The string in which to search for *char*
    :type string: string
    :returns: Index in *string* where *char* last appears (unescaped by a preceding "\\"), -1 if not found
    :rtype: int

    Finds the first occurrence of *char* in *string* in which *char* is
    not present as an escaped character.

    '''
    first_pos = -1
    pos = len(string)
    while pos > 0:
        pos = string[:pos].rfind(char)
        if pos == -1:
            return first_pos
        num_backslashes = 0
        test_index = pos - 1
        while test_index >= 0 and string[test_index] == '\\':
            num_backslashes += 1
            test_index -= 1

Read all three files in full (303 units, with 4 nested functions folded into their enclosing units). Fifteen units are reported as leads for a later check. Line numbers were taken from the numbered reads.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/describe.py::get_resolved_jbors (lines 289-315)
 - C8.S4, lines 296-297: for every JBOR in an execution's inputs it calls job_describe on the producing job (a full describe, including output) and stores only that one field. Several inputs usually come from the same upstream job, and print_execution_desc (lines 891-893) calls this once per input, so the same job is re-described once per JBOR. The resolved_jbors dedup at line 294 is keyed by JBOR string, not by job.
 - C4.S2, line 290: the top-level `resolved_thing == orig_thing` deep comparison repeats the `!=` test the caller already made at line 892, and each recursion level repeats it on its subtree.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/resolver.py::resolve_multiple_existing_paths (lines 941-1017)
 - C9.S1, lines 988-989 (via _check_resolution_needed, line 703): non-ID paths are batched into one dxpy.resolve_data_objects call, but every DX-ID path gets its own /<id>/describe request inside the loop. A bulk describe wrapper exists (api.py:1339, system_describe_data_objects); whether its fields match what is needed is unchecked. The sequential pattern could also be C11.S5.
 - C9.S1, line 997: each glob path gets its own find_data_objects call, same pattern.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/resolver.py::resolve_job_ref (lines 566-619)
 - C9.S1, lines 602-603: for an array-valued output, one /<file>/describe request per element, issued sequentially in a list comprehension. The element count is unbounded and a bulk describe could return them in one trip.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/resolver.py::resolve_container_id_or_name (lines 364-409)
 - C9.S2, line 388: find_projects(..., describe=True) asks the server for a full describe of every matching project, but the function reads only 'id' and 'level' from each result. The describe payload crosses the wire and is discarded.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/resolver.py::object_exists_in_project (lines 202-218)
 - C9.S2, line 218: calls /<obj>/describe only to read the 'project' field, which fetches the full describe. The codebase already passes a "fields" selector in describe calls (describe.py:653), so the request could be narrowed.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/resolver.py::resolve_path (lines 427-564)
 - C1.S4, line 483: under _DX_FUSE, xattr(path) is evaluated twice in one expression, each a filesystem extended-attribute read; one local would serve both.
 - C1.S4, line 535: get_last_pos_of_char(':', path) is recomputed though the same value is already in last_colon from line 515.
 - C4.S2, line 504: is_hashid(path) reruns the same regex after is_container_id(path) at line 502 already returned False for it.
 - Per-path cost is small, so these are minor.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/resolver.py::_check_resolution_needed (lines 622-723)
 - C9.S2, line 704 (low confidence): for globalworkflow IDs, dxpy.append_underlying_workflow_describe (src/python/dxpy/__init__.py:1031-1033) adds one workflow describe per region on every call, even when the caller needs only the id. Not checked whether callers read that output.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/resolver.py::_resolve_global_entity (lines 836-893)
 - C9.S2, lines 836 and 885-891 (low confidence): describe defaults to True, so every matched object is fully described. The TODO at lines 870-873 says the same. Not checked which callers use the describe output.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/resolver.py::_maybe_convert_stringified_dxlink (lines 412-424)
 - C4.S6, line 414: json.loads runs on every path. For ordinary paths such as "project-...:/folder/file" it raises a decode error that the bare except (line 422) swallows, so an exception is raised on the common path. A cheap leading-"{" check (C4.S7) would skip it.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/resolver.py::get_last_pos_of_char (lines 240-265)
 - C6.S2, line 255: each iteration copies the prefix string[:pos] to call rfind. str.rfind(char, 0, pos) searches the same range without the copy, so the cost is O(occurrences x length). Overlaps C10.S2.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/resolver.py::get_first_pos_of_char (lines 267-293)
 - C6.S2, line 283: same per-iteration prefix copy as get_last_pos_of_char, and it visits every occurrence. Overlaps C10.S2.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/resolver.py::split_unescaped (lines 295-321)
 - C6.S2, line 313: calls get_last_pos_of_char on string[:lastpos] each iteration, so the string is re-copied and rescanned per separator. Low impact because paths and inputs are short.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/resolver.py::parse_input_keyval (lines 1360-1369)
 - C1.S5, line 1365: split_unescaped('=', keyeqval) builds the full list of pieces, then only [0] is used, though the first unescaped '=' position is already known from line 1362. Negligible per CLI call. Edge cases with a leading '=' may differ, so check before changing.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/describe.py::get_find_executions_string (lines 1194-1266)
 - C1.S4, lines 1235 and 1259: the same DELIMITER('\n' + (u'│ ' if ... else ...)) expression is built twice, once appended to result at 1235 and once as prefix at 1259. Trivial cost.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/utils/describe.py::render_bundleddepends (lines 317-336)
 - C9.S1, lines 326 and 329 (low confidence): per bundle, two sequential API calls (file get_properties, then a record describe just to read its name). Bundles per applet are few, so the cost is small.

Considered and not reported, so the later check need not redo them:
- api.py: all generated wrappers. Each is one Python call forwarding to a network request, so C2.S1 is not on a hot path. The `input_params={}` defaults do not accumulate, because DXHTTPRequest serializes its data argument and does not mutate it (src/python/dxpy/__init__.py:553). The shallow copy in Nonce.update_nonce on run/new calls is small and per-call.
- resolver.py resolve_job_ref `describe={}` default: only 'project' is written, it is overwritten each call, and no in-repo caller uses the default.
- resolver.py resolve_multiple_existing_paths calls dxpy.resolve_data_objects with an empty list when nothing is batched. No API request is made, because the batching loop in bindings/search.py is empty for an empty list.
- describe.py format_currency calls locale.setlocale per currency field. That is a handful per describe.
- describe.py printable_ssh_host_key spawns ssh-keygen once per execution describe. This is needed work.

Most reported leads are small string-level or single-call costs. The strongest are the per-object API round trips: C8.S4 in get_resolved_jbors, and C9.S1 in resolve_multiple_existing_paths and resolve_job_ref.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/__init__.py::_get_pool_manager (lines 246-284)
 - C8.S2, lines 271-284: when cert_file, verify, or DX_CA_CERT is set, every call builds a new urllib3 PoolManager or ProxyManager and never caches it. DXHTTPRequest calls this once per attempt (line 591), so each request gets fresh TCP/TLS connections instead of reusing a pool. The comment at lines 269-270 says the pool should be cached.
 - C8.S2, lines 248-256: the default_pool_args dict and its os.environ check are rebuilt on every call, including the common case where the cached _pool_manager is returned at line 267 and the dict is thrown away.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/__init__.py::DXHTTPRequest (lines 469-817)
 - C6.S1, line 727: in the uncommon-pool branch, `_get_pool_manager(**pool_args).clear()` builds a fresh pool manager and clears it, which does nothing, while the pool that held the failed connection is never touched. The cached branch's clear is intentional (comment at 724-726), so only the uncommon branch is in question.
 - C1.S5, line 729 (low): exception_msg is formatted for every exception, including a terminal DXAPIError that is re-raised without reading it (the logging at 791-795 is skipped for DXAPIError).

UNIT src/python/dxpy/__init__.py::append_underlying_workflow_describe (lines 1024-1039)
 - C11.S5, lines 1035-1038: one workflow_describe round-trip per region, run in series. The calls are independent, so the waits could overlap. C9.S1 is an equally good card.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/__init__.py::DXHTTPOAuth2.__call__ (lines 824-830)
 - C8.S2, lines 826-827 (low): the Authorization value is rebuilt and encoded on every request, though security_context is fixed in __init__.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/app_builder.py::upload_resources (lines 247-482)
 - C1.S5, lines 316-405 and 429-434: the full uncompressed tar, with every file's bytes written at line 399, is built before the existing-bundle check. The checksum depends only on mode and mtime, which os.walk already yields. When a matching bundle exists (lines 429-434), the tar build was wasted; it is only needed on the upload branch.
 - C6.S2, lines 318-319 and 441-455: the data is copied twice, once into an uncompressed tar and again into a gzip temp file. One gzip-mode tar write would do it in one pass.
 - C3.S1, lines 447-451 (low): the copy runs in 8 KiB read/write iterations in Python. A larger buffer or shutil.copyfileobj means fewer interpreter iterations.
 - C1.S4, lines 371 and 373 (low): os.lstat(true_filename) is followed by os.path.islink(true_filename), which lstats the same path again. The result at 371 already says whether it is a link.
 - C10.S2, line 288 (low): `len(os.listdir(resources_dir)) > 0` builds the whole listing just to test for emptiness.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/app_builder.py::is_link_local (lines 192-217)
 - C3.S5, lines 208-215 (low): once is_local becomes False the answer is settled, but the loop keeps calling os.path.abspath(os.path.join(...)) for each remaining part. An early return would skip that.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/app_builder.py::_create_app (lines 773-952)
 - C6.S7, lines 774 and 783-794: the default `inherited_metadata={}` becomes app_spec when src_dir is falsy (line 783) and is then mutated (update at 785, billTo at 788, version at 794). State accumulates across calls that share the default. This is also a correctness hazard.
 - C1.S5, line 779 (low): json.dumps of the full app spec, including the inlined README, is built as a log argument.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/app_builder.py::create_app_multi_region (lines 739-754)
 - C6.S7, line 740: the same shared mutable default is declared here and passed through to _create_app.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/app_builder.py::_get_applet_spec (lines 127-135)
 - C8.S4, lines 129-130 (low): dxapp.json is opened, parsed and validated again on each call. A build reads it about three times (lines 280, 499 and 190, called from scripts/dx_build_app.py lines 888, 902 and 927). The file is small, so the cost is small.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/workflow_builder.py::_get_validated_json_for_build_or_update (lines 353-373)
 - C6.S2, line 359 (low): deep-copies json_spec again, although its caller _get_validated_json already deep-copied it at line 316. Two full deep traversals of the same spec in one build.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/workflow_builder.py::_assert_executable_regions_match (lines 376-418)
 - C8.S4, lines 389-409 (moderate): each stage's executable is described afresh. Applet stages get a DXApplet and a DXProject describe (391-392), and app stages get an app_describe (398). A workflow that uses one app in many stages, or many applets in one project, repeats the same fetches with no memo for the build.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/workflow_builder.py::_create_temporary_projects (lines 473-500)
 - C11.S5, lines 487-499 (low): one project_new round-trip per region, run in series. The calls are independent.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/workflow_builder.py::_build_underlying_workflows (lines 503-527)
 - C11.S5, lines 513-520 (low): one workflow_new per region, in series, each sending the full spec (including inlined docs). The operations are independent.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/workflow_builder.py::_build_global_workflow (lines 530-592)
 - C6.S2, lines 563-567 (low): a deepcopy of the final spec exists only to delete two keys for printing. A comprehension excluding them would do. Deepcopy does not copy strings, so the cost is container traversal only.
 - C1.S5, line 568 (low): json.dumps(print_spec) is built eagerly as a logger.info argument.

 - C5.S4, line 74 (low): the spec is serialised to JSON text, edited with a regex, and parsed back. A dict-to-dict pass would avoid the representation round trip. It runs once per global-workflow build.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/executable_builder.py::get_permitted_regions (lines 230-239)
 - C8.S4, line 236: issues DXHTTPRequest('/<billTo>/describe'). For an org billTo, get_valid_bill_to (lines 116-117) already called org_describe on the same org earlier in the same build (workflow_builder.py lines 684-685). The second fetch could reuse the first.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/executable_builder.py::assert_consistent_reg_options (lines 194-228)
 - C3.S2, line 212 (low): set(regional_options_list[0][1].keys()) is rebuilt on every pass of the region loop. The value does not change across iterations.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/executable_builder.py::verify_developer_rights (lines 130-180)
 - C8.S2, line 154 (low): the collections.namedtuple class is constructed on every call. Class construction costs far more than instance creation. It runs once per build, so the cost is small; it could live at module level.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/asset_builder.py::build_asset (lines 181-288)
 - C9.S1, line 262 (low to moderate): wait_on_done(interval=1) polls the job state once per second for the whole asset build. The wait_on_done default is 2 seconds (bindings/dxjob.py line 311). A long build means hundreds of state queries.
 - C1.S5, line 197 (low, may be intentional): the dxpy.api.system_whoami() result is discarded. It reads as an auth preflight, so it may be deliberate.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/system_requirements.py::SystemRequirementsDict.__init__ (lines 25-38)
 - C6.S2, line 38: every construction deep-copies entrypoints. Several callers pass freshly built dicts (override_cluster_spec line 168, override_spec line 178, __add__ line 204), so those are second deep copies of new data. The copy is justified for from_sys_requirements, which passes the caller's dict.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/system_requirements.py::SystemRequirementsDict.override_cluster_spec (lines 101-168)
 - C6.S2, line 145 (low): deep-copies all of self.entrypoints, then drops entries without clusterSpec or not requested (lines 148, 151-152). Those entries are copied for nothing.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/ssh_tunnel_app_support.py::get_notebook_app_versions (lines 80-86)
 - C9.S3, lines 84-85: find_apps is called without describe=True, although the search supports it (bindings/search.py, find_global_executables). Then dxpy.describe runs once per returned app, an N+1 pattern with one extra round-trip per notebook version.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/ssh_tunnel_app_support.py::poll_for_server_running (lines 43-62)
 - C9.S2, lines 49 and 55 (low): the full job description (all fields) is fetched every 5 seconds, though the loop reads only tags and state. A fields filter would shrink each response.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/dxlog.py::DXLogHandler.__init__ (lines 41-60)
 - C6.S6, lines 47-50 (low, error path): two AF_UNIX sockets are created before the path checks at lines 52-55, which can raise DXError. On that raise the sockets are never closed, and close() does not run because construction never completes.

UNIT src/python/dxpy/dxlog.py::DXLogHandler.truncate_message (lines 71-82)
 - C7.S1, lines 78-79: when the message is too long, the loop drops one byte per iteration and re-serialises the whole string with json.dumps each time. Messages that expand a lot in JSON (quotes, newlines, non-ASCII escapes) can take thousands of iterations, each over about 8 KB.
 - C1.S4, lines 74 and 96 (low): the message is JSON-encoded here for its length and again in emit (line 96) for the record.

Side notes, not energy: __init__.py line 868 writes bytes into a StringIO in the sub-chunk fallback of _dxhttp_read_range, which would raise TypeError. system_requirements.py line 59 constructs DXError without raising it, so the ValueError path returns None silently. ssh_tunnel_app_support.py line 137 misplaces the format arguments, which drops the '-y', '--brief', '--allow-ssh' and '--instance-type' flags from the run_loupe command. ssh_tunnel_app_support.py lines 123-126 leave remote_port undefined for notebook types other than jupyter.

(b) Total units read: 122 functions and methods, each read in full. Nothing in exceptions.py or compat.py was reported.

Read all 20 files and all 113 functions and methods. 22 units are reported as leads. The strongest cluster is the Dataset descriptor re-fetch, the quadratic list concatenation in cohort filters, and the per-call manifest download in `retrieve_bins`. Most other reports are weak and marked as such.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/bindings/apollo/dataset.py::Dataset.descriptor_file_dict (lines 40-57)
 - C8.S2, lines 43-45 and 55-57: no caching, so every access downloads the descriptor file, gunzips it and JSON-parses it again. The sibling `visualize_info` (lines 59-66) caches on the object, and `dxpy` `DXFile.read` has only a URL cache, not a content cache, so the cost recurs.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/bindings/apollo/dataset.py::Dataset.assays_info_dict (lines 89-111)
 - C8.S4, line 91: reads the uncached `descriptor_file_dict` on every property access, so each reference is a full download and parse. `dataset_utilities.py:1475` touches it three times in one condition. Weak: lines 94-104 re-index `assays[index]` five times per iteration (C8.S3).

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/bindings/apollo/dataset.py::Dataset.assay_info_dict (lines 113-117)
 - C8.S4, line 114: each call re-evaluates the uncached `assays_info_dict`, so each lookup costs one full descriptor download. The method has one caller in-repo (`dataset_utilities.py:1578`), so the impact is small in practice.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/bindings/apollo/dataset.py::Dataset.assay_names_list (lines 119-124)
 - C8.S4 and C1.S4, lines 121-122: `self.assays_info_dict` is read twice (the `if` test and the loop), so each call does two full descriptor downloads. `is_assay_name_valid` (126-127) inherits this, and `dataset_utilities.py:1462, 1468, 1664` call these methods.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/bindings/apollo/dataset.py::Dataset.assay_index (lines 129-134)
 - C8.S4, line 130: one uncached `assays_info_dict` access, so one full descriptor download per call. No caller in `src/` was found.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/bindings/apollo/data_transformations.py::transform_to_expression_matrix (lines 2-57)
 - C1.S4, lines 42-46: per input row, `entry["sample_id"]` is subscripted two or three times and `entry["feature_id"]` twice. The matrix can be very large, so this is small per row but real in total. Weak to moderate.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/bindings/apollo/vizserver_filters_from_json_parser.py::JSONFiltersValidator.__init__ (lines 32-66)
 - C5.S1, lines 39-66, used at line 231: `SUPPORTED_VIZSERVER_CONDITIONS` is a 26-item list tested with `not in` for every keyed list item, where a set would answer each test in O(1). Weak, because N is tiny.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/bindings/apollo/vizserver_filters_from_json_parser.py::JSONFiltersValidator.parse_v1 (lines 82-171)
 - C4.S4, lines 128, 141, 153: three consecutive `if`s test `current_properties` for list, dict and None, which are exclusive in fact, and all three still run after a match. Weak.
 - C1.S1, lines 139, 151, 166: the `filters = None` stores are never read, since the next read follows a reassignment. Weak.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/cohort_filter_payload.py::generate_pheno_filter (lines 5-83)
 - C7.S1, lines 37 and 39: `reduce(lambda_for_list_conv, primary_filter["values"], [])` with the lambda from `dataset_utilities.py:1750-1754` (`a+[str(b)]`, or int/float) copies the accumulated list at every step, so building N IDs is O(N²). Cohorts can hold many IDs. `dataset_utilities.py:1758` runs the same quadratic reduce, outside my files.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/filter_to_payload.py::location_filter (lines 101-139)
 - C8.S3, line 131: `"{}$a_id".format(table)` and the chain `location_aid_filter[...][0]["geno_bins"]` are rebuilt or re-resolved for every location. Weak, because validation caps locations at 100.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/filter_to_payload.py::final_payload (lines 201-284)
 - C8.S2, lines 236-255: reads and parses a static package asset (`return_columns_*.json`) on every call, although the same module caches `column_conversion` and `column_conditions` once at import (lines 15-25).
 - C3.S5, lines 265-270: the `sample_id` scan keeps going after its answer is known. Weak, since the field list is short.
 - C10.S2, line 282: `list(f.keys())[0]` allocates a list per field just to read the first key, where `next(iter(f))` would not. The same pattern is at `somatic_filter_payload.py:288`. Weak.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/filter_to_payload.py::validate_JSON (lines 287-307)
 - C1.S1, lines 293-297: the schema asset is opened, read and JSON-parsed into `json_schema`, which is never used. The only use, `validate(filter, json_schema)` at line 305, is commented out, and the note at line 299 says jsonschema is disabled. Each validation pays for a file open and parse with no effect.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/germline_utils.py::harmonize_germline_sql (lines 121-137)
 - C8.S2, lines 126-127: opens and parses `return_columns_genotype.json` on each call, always the same asset. Weak, since it runs once per genotype-only query.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/germline_utils.py::harmonize_germline_results (lines 140-153)
 - C6.S2, lines 144-153: builds a second full copy of every result row (a new dict per row, two lookups per field). The input rows are not used afterwards (`dataset_utilities.py:1093` only extends them into `ordered_results`), so the copy doubles peak memory. Filling in place would avoid it, but the key order would change, so check the consumer first.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/germline_utils.py::infer_genotype_type (lines 265-305)
 - C8.S3, lines 297 and 301: `loci_dict[locus]["samples"]` and `loci_dict[locus]["entry"]` are re-resolved inside the per-sample loop, which runs samples × loci times. Hoisting the locus record and its set out of the inner loop would remove the repeats.
 - C6.S2, line 305: `result_entries + inferred_entries` copies the whole result list once more. Weak.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/input_validation.py::is_list_of_strings (lines 26-37)
 - C4.S2, line 31, inside the loop at lines 29-36: `python_version == 2` is settled before the loop but tested for every item. Called on lists up to 1000 entries. Weak, one comparison per item.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/input_validation.py::validate_infer_flags (lines 231-261)
 - C1.S5, line 243: the f-string `ingestion_parameters_str` is built on every call but used only in the two error branches (lines 251 and 260). On the success path it is a resultless computation. Weak, since it runs once per invocation.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/input_validation_somatic.py::is_list_of_strings (lines 10-21)
 - C4.S2, line 15, inside the loop at lines 13-20: the same settled-before-the-loop test as in `input_validation.py`.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/retrieve_bins.py::retrieve_bins (lines 7-51)
 - C8.S4, lines 12, 23 and 33-36: every call does `dxpy.describe(project)` (12), a `describe` of the manifest entry to choose the file (23), and a `dx cat` subprocess that downloads the whole genome-bins JSON and parses it (33-36). Nothing is cached across calls, though the same manifest is fetched for each gene, symbol or feature key (`filter_to_payload.py:89` through `retrieve_geno_bins` at lines 28-38, and `somatic_filter_payload.py:100` through lines 44-61, up to three times per somatic assay). Any cache must copy the result, because line 44 `bin.pop("strand")` mutates the parsed dict.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/somatic_filter_payload.py::retrieve_geno_bins (lines 44-61)
 - C5.S1, line 58: membership test against the 24-item `chrs` list for every returned bin, where a set would do. Weak, since bins per gene are few.
 - C6.S2, lines 54-60: builds `updated_bins` as a copy when the bins could be edited in place and returned. Weak.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/somatic_filter_payload.py::basic_filter (lines 63-109)
 - C1.S5, lines 84-86: the fallback `"variant_read_optimized${}".format(friendly_name)` is formatted on every call, even when the key is found. Weak.
 - C1.S1, line 80: the incoming `table` argument is overwritten immediately and never read. Weak.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/dx_extract_utils/somatic_filter_payload.py::location_filter (lines 111-158)
 - C8.S3, lines 147 and 150-151: a linear `chr not in chrs` scan of a 24-item list per location, and re-resolution of `location_aid_filter["variant_read_optimized$allele_id"][0]["geno_bins"]` per location. Weak.

Noted outside the energy scope: `apollo/vizserver_filters_from_json_parser.py:589-590` sets `merged_filters[key] = []` before extending, so when the same key appears in two consecutive filter items the first item's conditions are dropped. This is a correctness issue, not an energy one.

Considered and not reported: the mutable default `values=[]` in both `basic_filter` functions is never mutated, so nothing accumulates. The intermediate dicts in `build_partial_overlap_genobin_filters` are kept for Python 2 compatibility, as its own comment explains. The CLI-only validators in `cmd_line_options_validator.py` run once per invocation over about 13 arguments.

The nine files are read in full and I checked the callees that decide the cost of the leads below. Nothing was edited or run. Line numbers are from the Read output.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/output_handling.py::write_expression_output (lines 9-164)
 - C3.S2, lines 126-128: `set(COLUMN_NAMES)` is rebuilt inside the per-row generator for every row, although `COLUMN_NAMES` is fixed after line 124. The cost is rows times columns of set construction on top of the writer pass. Strength: medium-high for large extracts.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/scripts/dx_build_app.py::_check_file_syntax (lines 269-342)
 - C1.S5, lines 284-291 (nested `check_python`): `py_compile.compile` writes a .pyc into the temp dir and then unlinks it; only the syntax result is used. An in-memory `compile()` of the source read once would do the same check with no file write. Strength: medium.
 - C1.S5, lines 310-324 (weak): a .py file is opened to read its first line, opened again for the readability test at 324, then opened again by the checker. Weak.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/scripts/dx_build_app.py::_check_suggestions (lines 99-155)
 - C1.S1, lines 126 and 148: `dnanexus_link` is bound to the full `dxpy.describe` payload and never read. Only the 404 existence check matters, so the full object description is fetched and discarded for each suggestion. Strength: low-medium.
 - C1.S5, line 140: `project_describe` result is discarded; only existence matters. Line 110 also requests `permissions` even when `publish` is False. Strength: low.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/scripts/dx_build_app.py::build_and_upload_locally (lines 758-993)
 - C8.S4, lines 845-847: for `applet` with `-d` destination, `working_project` was already described at lines 793-795 (same project, same `region` field). The second `project_describe` repeats it. Strength: low-medium.
 - C1.S5, lines 975-976: `app_describe` is fetched unconditionally but is used only when `not brief` (977-982) or `return_object_dump` (984). A brief, non-JSON build wastes the call. Strength: low-medium.
 - C8.S4, line 765 (weak): `dxapp.json` is re-parsed here, after `_verify_app_source_dir` and `_lint` already parsed it. Valid only if `dxpy.app_builder.build` (line 764) may change the file.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/scripts/dx_build_app.py::build_app_from (lines 699-755)
 - C1.S5, line 746: `app_describe` is always fetched but is used only for the non-brief log lines (748-753) and when `return_object_dump` is set (755). Strength: low.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/scripts/dx_build_app.py::_build_app_remote (lines 507-696)
 - C9.S1, line 681: `wait_on_done(interval=1)` polls the job state every second for the whole remote build when `watch` is False. Each poll is a describe call (dxjob.py lines 379-396). The library default is `interval=2` (dxjob.py line 311). Strength: medium-low.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/scripts/dx_build_app.py::_build_app (lines 1033-1215)
 - C10.S2, lines 1191-1192: `subprocess.check_output(["dx", "upload", ...])` starts a new dx CLI process to upload the source tree. The same file already uses in-process `dxpy.upload_local_file` at line 647. Strength: low-medium; check whether in-process directory upload can replace it.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/scripts/dx_build_app.py::build (lines 1218-1239)
 - C10.S2, line 1235 (weak): starts a new `dx run` process for the executable the in-process API could launch.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/scripts/dx_build_app.py::_lint (lines 157-236)
 - C6.S6, line 171 (weak): `json.load(open(...))` never closes the file explicitly. CPython closes it on refcount drop, so the energy effect is small; only relevant on non-refcounting runtimes.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/scripts/dx_build_app.py::_verify_app_source_dir_impl (lines 345-452)
 - C8.S4, line 354 (weak): re-opens and re-parses the `dxapp.json` that `_lint` already parsed at line 350, because `_lint` takes a path, not the parsed dict.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/workflow.py::add_stage (lines 93-128)
 - C8.S4, line 128: `dxworkflow.describe()` makes a second API call after `DXWorkflow.add_stage`, which already calls `self.describe()` in its `finally` (bindings/dxworkflow.py lines 241-242). Strength: medium-low.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/workflow.py::update_stage (lines 205-280)
 - C1.S6, line 213: `dxworkflow.editVersion` is a lazy attribute (bindings/__init__.py lines 94-101) that triggers a describe on a fresh handle. It runs before the no-updates early return at 220-224, so a no-op call still pays for it. Strength: low-medium.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/workflow.py::update_workflow (lines 179-203)
 - C1.S5, line 181: the workflow is resolved over the API before the no-updates check at 183-186. On that path the result is used only for validation. Strength: low.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/cp.py::cp (lines 109-160)
 - C9.S2, line 116: existence of the destination is tested by listing all subfolders of `dest_path` (`only='folders'`). That pulls the whole listing to learn one fact. Strength: low-medium; no cheaper existence endpoint was checked.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/cp.py::cp_to_noexistent_destination (lines 33-106)
 - C9.S1, lines 99-103: one sequential rename request per matched result. Only relevant with `--all` and multiple matches. Strength: weak.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/download.py::download (lines 187-285)
 - C9.S2, line 228: `dxpy.list_subfolders(project, parent_folder, recurse=False)` runs for every path argument, fetching every subfolder of the parent. This happens even when the path already matched a file and has no glob, and only one name or pattern is kept. Strength: medium-low.
 - C8.S4, lines 251-254: `object_exists_in_project` makes one describe call per matching file to confirm membership in the explicit project. Verify whether `resolve_existing_path` already guarantees this for explicit-project paths; `--lightweight` exists to skip the check. Strength: low-medium.
 - C3.S2, lines 193-204: the resolver kwargs, including the constant `describe` dict, are rebuilt on every path argument. Strength: weak.
 - C1.S4, lines 215 and 217: `is_jbor_str(path)` is computed twice. Strength: weak.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/download.py::_rel2abs (lines 149-157)
 - C1.S4, line 154: `os.path.join(wd, path)` is computed twice in one expression, where one local would serve both. Strength: weak; runs once per path argument.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/download.py::download_one_database_file (lines 107-135)
 - C1.S5, lines 108 and 110: the `.format()` strings for debug logging are built eagerly, even when debug logging is off. Strength: weak; once per database file.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/download.py::do_debug (lines 102-103)
 - C2.S1, lines 102-103: a pure pass-through to `logging.debug`. Not on a hot path. Strength: weak.

UNIT /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/org.py::find_orgs (lines 196-210)
 - C3.S2, line 208: `DELIMITER(args.delimiter)` is loop-invariant but is re-evaluated for each org in the loop at 205-210. Strength: weak; the number of orgs is small.

(a) Files covered, all read in full:
- /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/scripts/dx_build_app.py
- /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/cp.py
- /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/download.py
- /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/help_messages.py
- /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/__init__.py
- /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/output_handling.py
- /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/parsers.py
- /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/org.py
- /home/javad/energy-run/dx-toolkit/src/python/dxpy/cli/workflow.py

Callees read for cost: dxpy bindings `dxjob.py` (`wait_on_done`, `_get_state`), `dxworkflow.py` (`add_stage`, `get_stage`, `describe` refresh), `bindings/__init__.py` (`__getattr__`), `utils/resolver.py` (`object_exists_in_project`, `get_first_pos_of_char`), `utils/printing.py`.

(b) Units read: 83. Nested functions were counted inside their enclosing unit. `help_messages.py` has no functions.

(c) Units reported: 21.

Not reported, and why:
- Module-level import-time work, not counted as units: `parsers.py` builds about 20 argparse parsers and around 60 `fill()` calls on every dx invocation, and `help_messages.py` calls `fill()` at import. Both are C1.S6 candidates at most, probably milliseconds, and unmeasured.
- `download.py` `_verify`, `_which` and `_ensure_local_dir` have no callers in the repo, so they cost nothing at runtime. `_verify` would shell out to md5sum if it were ever called.
- Once-per-invocation trivia was skipped: a repeated `.lower()` in `org.get_user_id`, and thin wrappers in `parsers.py` such as `_parse_inst_type`.
- `org.add_membership` and `remove_membership` use an API membership check that is required, so they are not waste. `download._is_glob` uses an escape-aware scan, and a plain membership test would change behaviour.

1	# The taxonomy, in full
2	
3	An **energy smell** is code that spends energy on work the program does not
4	need, and that a specific refactoring can remove without changing what the
5	program does. This taxonomy names them: twelve categories, sixty-five root
6	causes.
7	
8	This page is what to look for in step 1. Read it before you read the code, and
9	keep it beside you: of every function, ask whether any of these is happening
10	there. The **category table** says what each family of waste covers; the
11	**root cause table** below it lists all sixty-five, one line each — enough to
12	recognise one, not enough to decide it. Deciding is step 2, with the root
13	cause's card.
14	
15	Cards live at `reference/categories/<ID>.md` — a category's root causes, with
16	the repair for each — and `reference/root-causes/<ID>.<S>.md`, which open at
17	`step.py done 1`.
18	
19	## Categories
20	
21	| ID | Category | Covers | Card |
22	|---|---|---|---|
23	| **C1** | Redundant Computation | Energy waste from executing work that does not contribute to the program's required output or that leaves program state unchanged | `reference/categories/C1.md` (8) |
24	| **C2** | Unnecessary Call Overhead | Energy waste from extra layers of function calls, method delegation, or dynamic dispatch that add overhead without proportional benefit | `reference/categories/C2.md` (3) |
25	| **C3** | Inefficient Iteration Patterns | Energy waste from loops that perform more per-iteration work than necessary, iterate more times than required, use suboptimal loop constructs, or fail to terminate correctly | `reference/categories/C3.md` (7) |
26	| **C4** | Inefficient Control Flow | Energy waste from branching, conditions, or dispatch logic that performs unnecessary checks, uses suboptimal evaluation order, or employs patterns that prevent interpreter optimization | `reference/categories/C4.md` (8) |
27	| **C5** | Suboptimal Data Structures | Energy waste from choosing, provisioning, or converting data structures that do not match the workload's access pattern or size requirements | `reference/categories/C5.md` (4) |
28	| **C6** | Unnecessary Memory Usage | Patterns that allocate, copy, retain, or leak memory beyond what the workload requires, increasing garbage collection overhead, memory-bus traffic, and system energy consumption | `reference/categories/C6.md` (7) |
29	| **C7** | Suboptimal Algorithmic | Energy waste from choosing an algorithm, decomposition, or computation strategy that explores more of the problem space than necessary or uses higher complexity than the problem requires | `reference/categories/C7.md` (5) |
30	| **C8** | Missing Reuse | Energy waste from failing to store and reuse results of expensive computations, lookups, or data fetches, causing the same work to be repeated across calls, requests, or access sites | `reference/categories/C8.md` (4) |
31	| **C9** | Inefficient External Data Access | Energy waste from inefficient interaction with external systems: databases, file systems, network services, and APIs | `reference/categories/C9.md` (4) |
32	| **C10** | Underused Language Primitives | Energy waste from not using available optimized language features, standard library functions, or runtime-specific constructs that would accomplish the same task more efficiently | `reference/categories/C10.md` (6) |
33	| **C11** | Inefficient Concurrency Management | Energy waste from thread/task misuse, synchronization overhead, contention, or failure to exploit available parallelism | `reference/categories/C11.md` (5) |
34	| **C12** | Poor Hardware Locality Usage | Energy waste driven by CPU and memory hierarchy behavior such as cache misses, branch misprediction, and suboptimal memory access patterns | `reference/categories/C12.md` (4) |
35	
36	## Every root cause, one line each
37	
38	### C1 — Redundant Computation
39	
40	| ID | Name | Looks for |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| **C1.S1** | Dead Code | a value computed and bound to a name that nothing ever reads |
43	| **C1.S2** | Redundant Assignment | a store that leaves the program's state exactly as it already was |
44	| **C1.S3** | Redundant Control Flow | a branch whose outcome is the same whichever way it goes |
45	| **C1.S4** | Repeated Computation | the same value computed twice in one scope, where one local would serve both |
46	| **C1.S5** | Resultless Computation | a computation run in full whose result nothing downstream actually needs |
47	| **C1.S6** | Unnecessary Initialization | setup done unconditionally that only one path actually needs |
48	| **C1.S7** | Unnecessary Variable | a name bound, read exactly once, and never needed again |
49	| **C1.S8** | Excessive Runtime-Management Calls | runtime housekeeping invoked far more often than anything needs it |
50	
51	### C2 — Unnecessary Call Overhead
52	
53	| ID | Name | Looks for |
54	|---|---|---|
55	| **C2.S1** | Unnecessary Method Delegation | a wrapper or property that forwards, adds nothing, and sits on a hot path |
56	| **C2.S2** | Missing Static Declaration | a method that never touches `self` and still pays to be bound to an instance |
57	| **C2.S3** | Excessive Modularization in Hot Path | a chain of thin layers whose frames cost more than the work at the bottom |
58	
59	### C3 — Inefficient Iteration Patterns
60	
61	| ID | Name | Looks for |
62	|---|---|---|
63	| **C3.S1** | Inefficient Iteration Construct | a loop written in a form that does more interpreter work per element than it needs to |
64	| **C3.S2** | Recomputing Loop-Invariant Values | an expression recomputed every iteration whose answer never changes |
65	| **C3.S3** | Inefficient Per-Iteration Setup | an object or resource created once per iteration that the whole loop could share |
66	| **C3.S4** | Inefficient Nested Iteration | an inner loop that searches, where a lookup would turn n*m into n+m |
67	| **C3.S5** | Missing Loop Early Exit | a loop that keeps going after its answer is already settled |
68	| **C3.S6** | Unfiltered Bulk Iteration | the whole collection processed when only a subset was ever wanted |
69	| **C3.S7** | Inefficient Array Mutation in Loop | a collection edited while it is being walked |
70	
71	### C4 — Inefficient Control Flow
72	
73	| ID | Name | Looks for |
74	|---|---|---|
75	| **C4.S1** | Poor Short-Circuit Ordering | a boolean chain that evaluates its expensive operand before the cheap one that usually decides |
76	| **C4.S2** | Redundant Conditional Evaluation | a test whose answer was already settled before it ran |
77	| **C4.S3** | Inefficient Conditional Nesting | a nest or chain of branches that tests more than it has to, where a lookup would test once |
78	| **C4.S4** | Missing Else-If | consecutive `if`s on one subject that are exclusive in fact but not in form |
79	| **C4.S5** | Expensive Comparison | a type check made per element where the answer never varies or the types could dispatch themselves |
80	| **C4.S6** | Expensive Exception Control Flow | an exception used as ordinary control flow, on a path where it is raised often |
81	| **C4.S7** | Missing Edge-Case Guards | a missing cheap test that would let a common trivial input skip the expensive path |
82	| **C4.S8** | Non-Idiomatic Condition | a condition spelled the long way round, missing the interpreter's fast path |
83	
84	### C5 — Suboptimal Data Structures
85	
86	| ID | Name | Looks for |
87	|---|---|---|
88	| **C5.S1** | Inefficient Data Structure Choice | a container whose type makes its most frequent operation the expensive one |
89	| **C5.S2** | Missing Helper Type | a collection searched again and again where one index built beside it would answer every question |
90	| **C5.S3** | Over-Provisioned Data Type | a representation heavier than the data it holds actually requires |
91	| **C5.S4** | Unnecessary Representation Change | a conversion between representations that the code on either side did not need |
92	
93	### C6 — Unnecessary Memory Usage
94	
95	| ID | Name | Looks for |
96	|---|---|---|
97	| **C6.S1** | Unnecessary Object | objects created and thrown away that never needed to exist |
98	| **C6.S2** | Unnecessary Copying | data duplicated when the original could have been used or changed in place |
99	| **C6.S3** | Unnecessary Data Materialization | a whole sequence built in memory when the consumer wanted it one element at a time |
100	| **C6.S4** | Oversized Data Retaining | something long-lived holding far more data than anything later reads |
101	| **C6.S5** | Over-Allocation | capacity reserved up front for data that never arrives |
102	| **C6.S6** | Leaked Resource Handles | a file, socket or connection acquired with nothing guaranteeing its release |
103	| **C6.S7** | Leaking Mutable Default Arguments | a mutable default argument that quietly accumulates across every call |
104	
105	### C7 — Suboptimal Algorithmic
106	
107	| ID | Name | Looks for |
108	|---|---|---|
109	| **C7.S1** | Suboptimal Algorithm Choice | an algorithm of worse complexity than the problem requires |
110	| **C7.S2** | Inefficient Problem Decomposition | a search exploring subproblems it could have pruned, reordered or reused |
111	| **C7.S3** | Avoidable Recursive Implementation | a recursion paying a frame per level where a loop would use one |
112	| **C7.S4** | Inefficient Operation Ordering | two commuting operations in the order that makes the expensive one see more data |
113	| **C7.S5** | Unsimplified Operation | an operation doing more work than an algebraic fact about its inputs requires |
114	
115	### C8 — Missing Reuse
116	
117	| ID | Name | Looks for |
118	|---|---|---|
119	| **C8.S1** | Missing Memoization Cache | a deterministic computation repeated across calls that a cache would answer |
120	| **C8.S2** | Missing Derived-Value Reuse | an expensive artefact derived again on every use instead of once for the process |
121	| **C8.S3** | Missing Local Lookup Caching | a name or attribute chain re-resolved every iteration for a value that never moves |
122	| **C8.S4** | Redundant Data Fetching | the same external data fetched again when the copy in memory was still good |
123	
124	### C9 — Inefficient External Data Access
125	
126	| ID | Name | Looks for |
127	|---|---|---|
128	| **C9.S1** | Fragmented I/O Calls | many small independent external operations where one bulk operation would do |
129	| **C9.S2** | Oversized Data Retrieval | more data pulled across a process boundary than the program ever consults |
130	| **C9.S3** | Inefficient Retrieval Paths | one fetch per row of an earlier fetch, where a join would have taken one trip |
131	| **C9.S4** | Expensive Query Pattern | a query whose shape makes the engine do far more work than the answer needs |
132	
133	### C10 — Underused Language Primitives
134	
135	| ID | Name | Looks for |
136	|---|---|---|
137	| **C10.S1** | Skipping Optimized Built-ins | a hand-written loop doing bulk work a C-level primitive already does |
138	| **C10.S2** | Inefficient Built-in Choice | one primitive used where a cheaper primitive computes the same answer |
139	| **C10.S3** | Missing Bulk Primitive Usage | a per-element call inside a loop that a single batched call would replace |
140	| **C10.S4** | Inefficient String Concatenation | a string grown with `+=` in a loop, where the target is aliased or the parts are many |
141	| **C10.S5** | Inefficient Scope Lookup | a global or builtin re-resolved through the module namespace on every iteration |
142	| **C10.S6** | Expensive Operator Overloads | an operator on a user-defined type dispatching and allocating once per element |
143	
144	### C11 — Inefficient Concurrency Management
145	
146	| ID | Name | Looks for |
147	|---|---|---|
148	| **C11.S1** | Excessive Lock Contention | a lock held across work that shares nothing, serialising what could overlap |
149	| **C11.S2** | Forced Serial Bottleneck | concurrency paid for in full while one shared resource serialises all of it |
150	| **C11.S3** | Leaked Background Threads | workers started and never stopped, accumulating for the life of the process |
151	| **C11.S4** | Blocking The Main Thread | a synchronous blocking call inside a coroutine, stopping every other task |
152	| **C11.S5** | Missed Parallelism Opportunities | independent work run one item at a time when the waits could have overlapped |
153	
154	### C12 — Poor Hardware Locality Usage
155	
156	| ID | Name | Looks for |
157	|---|---|---|
158	| **C12.S1** | Inefficient Large-Stride Traversal | a contiguous buffer traversed against the direction its memory is laid out in |
159	| **C12.S2** | Sparse Element Access | scattered reads into a large buffer, using one element of every cache line fetched |
160	| **C12.S3** | Unpredictable Branches | a data-dependent branch in a compiled hot loop that the CPU cannot predict |
161	| **C12.S4** | Inefficient Array Declaration Order | a declared struct whose field order puts cold data in front of hot data |
162	
163	## Using this well
164	
165	**Any category may apply to any code.** Nothing about a repository rules a
166	category in or out in advance. Work from what the code actually does.
167	
168	**Read the card, not the name, and not the line above.** These names are three
169	or four words long and several of them cover something narrower — or wider —
170	than they sound like. The one-line summaries here are index entries, precise
171	enough to recognise something by and not enough to decide anything from. The
172	card is the claim.
173	
174	**The index tells you what to look for, not what you will find.** A unit goes
175	on your list because of what its code does, not because a line here sounds
176	like it. Finding nothing in a category is a perfectly ordinary outcome.
177	
178	**Cards overlap.** When two root causes both describe what you repaired,
179	either attribution is fine — say which you chose.
180	
181	## What tools can and cannot contribute
182	
183	Any static rule, in any tool, recognises a syntactic shape that somebody
184	described in advance. That makes rules dependable about the shapes they know
185	and completely blind to everything else. Two consequences, and they point in
186	opposite directions:
187	
188	- **A rule firing has observed a pattern, not diagnosed a problem.** Every
189	  pattern in this taxonomy is the right thing to write somewhere, which is what
190	  each card's `Looks like it, but is not` section records.
191	  Some of what any rule reports is therefore wrong here, and saying which is
192	  part of the job.
193	- **A rule staying quiet has observed nothing.** Waste that lives in the
194	  arrangement of a program — work computed and discarded, a data shape that
195	  forces every later step to compensate, a query issued once per row — has no
196	  fixed syntactic shape at all, and is usually the expensive kind.
197	
198	Reading the code is the primary method here. Anything a tool tells you is a
199	second opinion to reconcile with what you already worked out.
200

1	# The taxonomy, in full
2	
3	An **energy smell** is code that spends energy on work the program does not
4	need, and that a specific refactoring can remove without changing what the
5	program does. This taxonomy names them: twelve categories, sixty-five root
6	causes.
7	
8	This page is what to look for in step 1. Read it before you read the code, and
9	keep it beside you: of every function, ask whether any of these is happening
10	there. The **category table** says what each family of waste covers; the
11	**root cause table** below it lists all sixty-five, one line each — enough to
12	recognise one, not enough to decide it. Deciding is step 2, with the root
13	cause's card.
14	
15	Cards live at `reference/categories/<ID>.md` — a category's root causes, with
16	the repair for each — and `reference/root-causes/<ID>.<S>.md`, which open at
17	`step.py done 1`.
18	
19	## Categories
20	
21	| ID | Category | Covers | Card |
22	|---|---|---|---|
23	| **C1** | Redundant Computation | Energy waste from executing work that does not contribute to the program's required output or that leaves program state unchanged | `reference/categories/C1.md` (8) |
24	| **C2** | Unnecessary Call Overhead | Energy waste from extra layers of function calls, method delegation, or dynamic dispatch that add overhead without proportional benefit | `reference/categories/C2.md` (3) |
25	| **C3** | Inefficient Iteration Patterns | Energy waste from loops that perform more per-iteration work than necessary, iterate more times than required, use suboptimal loop constructs, or fail to terminate correctly | `reference/categories/C3.md` (7) |
26	| **C4** | Inefficient Control Flow | Energy waste from branching, conditions, or dispatch logic that performs unnecessary checks, uses suboptimal evaluation order, or employs patterns that prevent interpreter optimization | `reference/categories/C4.md` (8) |
27	| **C5** | Suboptimal Data Structures | Energy waste from choosing, provisioning, or converting data structures that do not match the workload's access pattern or size requirements | `reference/categories/C5.md` (4) |
28	| **C6** | Unnecessary Memory Usage | Patterns that allocate, copy, retain, or leak memory beyond what the workload requires, increasing garbage collection overhead, memory-bus traffic, and system energy consumption | `reference/categories/C6.md` (7) |
29	| **C7** | Suboptimal Algorithmic | Energy waste from choosing an algorithm, decomposition, or computation strategy that explores more of the problem space than necessary or uses higher complexity than the problem requires | `reference/categories/C7.md` (5) |
30	| **C8** | Missing Reuse | Energy waste from failing to store and reuse results of expensive computations, lookups, or data fetches, causing the same work to be repeated across calls, requests, or access sites | `reference/categories/C8.md` (4) |
31	| **C9** | Inefficient External Data Access | Energy waste from inefficient interaction with external systems: databases, file systems, network services, and APIs | `reference/categories/C9.md` (4) |
32	| **C10** | Underused Language Primitives | Energy waste from not using available optimized language features, standard library functions, or runtime-specific constructs that would accomplish the same task more efficiently | `reference/categories/C10.md` (6) |
33	| **C11** | Inefficient Concurrency Management | Energy waste from thread/task misuse, synchronization overhead, contention, or failure to exploit available parallelism | `reference/categories/C11.md` (5) |
34	| **C12** | Poor Hardware Locality Usage | Energy waste driven by CPU and memory hierarchy behavior such as cache misses, branch misprediction, and suboptimal memory access patterns | `reference/categories/C12.md` (4) |
35	
36	## Every root cause, one line each
37	
38	### C1 — Redundant Computation
39	
40	| ID | Name | Looks for |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| **C1.S1** | Dead Code | a value computed and bound to a name that nothing ever reads |
43	| **C1.S2** | Redundant Assignment | a store that leaves the program's state exactly as it already was |
44	| **C1.S3** | Redundant Control Flow | a branch whose outcome is the same whichever way it goes |
45	| **C1.S4** | Repeated Computation | the same value computed twice in one scope, where one local would serve both |
46	| **C1.S5** | Resultless Computation | a computation run in full whose result nothing downstream actually needs |
47	| **C1.S6** | Unnecessary Initialization | setup done unconditionally that only one path actually needs |
48	| **C1.S7** | Unnecessary Variable | a name bound, read exactly once, and never needed again |
49	| **C1.S8** | Excessive Runtime-Management Calls | runtime housekeeping invoked far more often than anything needs it |
50	
51	### C2 — Unnecessary Call Overhead
52	
53	| ID | Name | Looks for |
54	|---|---|---|
55	| **C2.S1** | Unnecessary Method Delegation | a wrapper or property that forwards, adds nothing, and sits on a hot path |
56	| **C2.S2** | Missing Static Declaration | a method that never touches `self` and still pays to be bound to an instance |
57	| **C2.S3** | Excessive Modularization in Hot Path | a chain of thin layers whose frames cost more than the work at the bottom |
58	
59	### C3 — Inefficient Iteration Patterns
60	
61	| ID | Name | Looks for |
62	|---|---|---|
63	| **C3.S1** | Inefficient Iteration Construct | a loop written in a form that does more interpreter work per element than it needs to |
64	| **C3.S2** | Recomputing Loop-Invariant Values | an expression recomputed every iteration whose answer never changes |
65	| **C3.S3** | Inefficient Per-Iteration Setup | an object or resource created once per iteration that the whole loop could share |
66	| **C3.S4** | Inefficient Nested Iteration | an inner loop that searches, where a lookup would turn n*m into n+m |
67	| **C3.S5** | Missing Loop Early Exit | a loop that keeps going after its answer is already settled |
68	| **C3.S6** | Unfiltered Bulk Iteration | the whole collection processed when only a subset was ever wanted |
69	| **C3.S7** | Inefficient Array Mutation in Loop | a collection edited while it is being walked |
70	
71	### C4 — Inefficient Control Flow
72	
73	| ID | Name | Looks for |
74	|---|---|---|
75	| **C4.S1** | Poor Short-Circuit Ordering | a boolean chain that evaluates its expensive operand before the cheap one that usually decides |
76	| **C4.S2** | Redundant Conditional Evaluation | a test whose answer was already settled before it ran |
77	| **C4.S3** | Inefficient Conditional Nesting | a nest or chain of branches that tests more than it has to, where a lookup would test once |
78	| **C4.S4** | Missing Else-If | consecutive `if`s on one subject that are exclusive in fact but not in form |
79	| **C4.S5** | Expensive Comparison | a type check made per element where the answer never varies or the types could dispatch themselves |
80	| **C4.S6** | Expensive Exception Control Flow | an exception used as ordinary control flow, on a path where it is raised often |
81	| **C4.S7** | Missing Edge-Case Guards | a missing cheap test that would let a common trivial input skip the expensive path |
82	| **C4.S8** | Non-Idiomatic Condition | a condition spelled the long way round, missing the interpreter's fast path |
83	
84	### C5 — Suboptimal Data Structures
85	
86	| ID | Name | Looks for |
87	|---|---|---|
88	| **C5.S1** | Inefficient Data Structure Choice | a container whose type makes its most frequent operation the expensive one |
89	| **C5.S2** | Missing Helper Type | a collection searched again and again where one index built beside it would answer every question |
90	| **C5.S3** | Over-Provisioned Data Type | a representation heavier than the data it holds actually requires |
91	| **C5.S4** | Unnecessary Representation Change | a conversion between representations that the code on either side did not need |
92	
93	### C6 — Unnecessary Memory Usage
94	
95	| ID | Name | Looks for |
96	|---|---|---|
97	| **C6.S1** | Unnecessary Object | objects created and thrown away that never needed to exist |
98	| **C6.S2** | Unnecessary Copying | data duplicated when the original could have been used or changed in place |
99	| **C6.S3** | Unnecessary Data Materialization | a whole sequence built in memory when the consumer wanted it one element at a time |
100	| **C6.S4** | Oversized Data Retaining | something long-lived holding far more data than anything later reads |
101	| **C6.S5** | Over-Allocation | capacity reserved up front for data that never arrives |
102	| **C6.S6** | Leaked Resource Handles | a file, socket or connection acquired with nothing guaranteeing its release |
103	| **C6.S7** | Leaking Mutable Default Arguments | a mutable default argument that quietly accumulates across every call |
104	
105	### C7 — Suboptimal Algorithmic
106	
107	| ID | Name | Looks for |
108	|---|---|---|
109	| **C7.S1** | Suboptimal Algorithm Choice | an algorithm of worse complexity than the problem requires |
110	| **C7.S2** | Inefficient Problem Decomposition | a search exploring subproblems it could have pruned, reordered or reused |
111	| **C7.S3** | Avoidable Recursive Implementation | a recursion paying a frame per level where a loop would use one |
112	| **C7.S4** | Inefficient Operation Ordering | two commuting operations in the order that makes the expensive one see more data |
113	| **C7.S5** | Unsimplified Operation | an operation doing more work than an algebraic fact about its inputs requires |
114	
115	### C8 — Missing Reuse
116	
117	| ID | Name | Looks for |
118	|---|---|---|
119	| **C8.S1** | Missing Memoization Cache | a deterministic computation repeated across calls that a cache would answer |
120	| **C8.S2** | Missing Derived-Value Reuse | an expensive artefact derived again on every use instead of once for the process |
121	| **C8.S3** | Missing Local Lookup Caching | a name or attribute chain re-resolved every iteration for a value that never moves |
122	| **C8.S4** | Redundant Data Fetching | the same external data fetched again when the copy in memory was still good |
123	
124	### C9 — Inefficient External Data Access
125	
126	| ID | Name | Looks for |
127	|---|---|---|
128	| **C9.S1** | Fragmented I/O Calls | many small independent external operations where one bulk operation would do |
129	| **C9.S2** | Oversized Data Retrieval | more data pulled across a process boundary than the program ever consults |
130	| **C9.S3** | Inefficient Retrieval Paths | one fetch per row of an earlier fetch, where a join would have taken one trip |
131	| **C9.S4** | Expensive Query Pattern | a query whose shape makes the engine do far more work than the answer needs |
132	
133	### C10 — Underused Language Primitives
134	
135	| ID | Name | Looks for |
136	|---|---|---|
137	| **C10.S1** | Skipping Optimized Built-ins | a hand-written loop doing bulk work a C-level primitive already does |
138	| **C10.S2** | Inefficient Built-in Choice | one primitive used where a cheaper primitive computes the same answer |
139	| **C10.S3** | Missing Bulk Primitive Usage | a per-element call inside a loop that a single batched call would replace |
140	| **C10.S4** | Inefficient String Concatenation | a string grown with `+=` in a loop, where the target is aliased or the parts are many |
141	| **C10.S5** | Inefficient Scope Lookup | a global or builtin re-resolved through the module namespace on every iteration |

144	### C11 — Inefficient Concurrency Management
145	
146	| ID | Name | Looks for |
147	|---|---|---|
148	| **C11.S1** | Excessive Lock Contention | a lock held across work that shares nothing, serialising what could overlap |
149	| **C11.S2** | Forced Serial Bottleneck | concurrency paid for in full while one shared resource serialises all of it |
150	| **C11.S3** | Leaked Background Threads | workers started and never stopped, accumulating for the life of the process |
151	| **C11.S4** | Blocking The Main Thread | a synchronous blocking call inside a coroutine, stopping every other task |
152	| **C11.S5** | Missed Parallelism Opportunities | independent work run one item at a time when the waits could have overlapped |
153	
154	### C12 — Poor Hardware Locality Usage
155	
156	| ID | Name | Looks for |
157	|---|---|---|
158	| **C12.S1** | Inefficient Large-Stride Traversal | a contiguous buffer traversed against the direction its memory is laid out in |
159	| **C12.S2** | Sparse Element Access | scattered reads into a large buffer, using one element of every cache line fetched |
160	| **C12.S3** | Unpredictable Branches | a data-dependent branch in a compiled hot loop that the CPU cannot predict |
161	| **C12.S4** | Inefficient Array Declaration Order | a declared struct whose field order puts cold data in front of hot data |

163	## Using this well
164	
165	**Any category may apply to any code.** Nothing about a repository rules a
166	category in or out in advance. Work from what the code actually does.
167	
168	**Read the card, not the name, and not the line above.** These names are three
169	or four words long and several of them cover something narrower — or wider —
170	than they sound like. The one-line summaries here are index entries, precise
171	enough to recognise something by and not enough to decide anything from. The
172	card is the claim.
173	
174	**The index tells you what to look for, not what you will find.** A unit goes
175	on your list because of what its code does, not because a line here sounds
176	like it. Finding nothing in a category is a perfectly ordinary outcome.
177	
178	**Cards overlap.** When two root causes both describe what you repaired,
179	either attribution is fine — say which you chose.
180	
181	## What tools can and cannot contribute
182	
183	Any static rule, in any tool, recognises a syntactic shape that somebody
184	described in advance. That makes rules dependable about the shapes they know
185	and completely blind to everything else. Two consequences, and they point in
186	opposite directions:
187	
188	- **A rule firing has observed a pattern, not diagnosed a problem.** Every
189	  pattern in this taxonomy is the right thing to write somewhere, which is what
190	  each card's `Looks like it, but is not` section records.
191	  Some of what any rule reports is therefore wrong here, and saying which is
192	  part of the job.
193	- **A rule staying quiet has observed nothing.** Waste that lives in the
194	  arrangement of a program — work computed and discarded, a data shape that
195	  forces every later step to compensate, a query issued once per row — has no
196	  fixed syntactic shape at all, and is usually the expensive kind.
197	
198	Reading the code is the primary method here. Anything a tool tells you is a
199	second opinion to reconcile with what you already worked out.
